citation.title: Automated Annotation with Generative AI Requires Validation
citation.venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint arXiv:2306.00176v1 [cs.CL], dated 2 June 2023 (submitted 31 May 2023)

question: Whether and how researchers can use a generative LLM to annotate text, and how to validate its performance against expert human labels task by task. The paper argues validation is always needed and proposes a five-step workflow.
data: Replication of 27 annotation tasks across 11 non-public social science datasets from recent articles in high-impact journals, with the original human labels as ground truth. Slightly over 200,000 text samples were annotated with GPT-4 via the OpenAI API, for about $420 USD (p. 7). The paper does not classify organisations, and it does not mention fossil fuel links or a sample of about 1,250 organisations. The figure 1,250 appears only as the top of its suggested range for validation samples (p. 6, fn 7).
method: Every dimension is treated as a separate binary annotation task. The LLM uses the same codebook as the human coders, as its prompt. The authors compare LLM labels with human labels (accuracy, precision, recall, F1), make at most one round of codebook updates per task, and report results on held-out samples. Each sample is labelled at least seven times at temperature 0.6, giving a consistency score (proportion of repeats matching the modal label). The paper says the code is available at github.com/npangakis/gpt_annotate (p. 4, fn 5).

definitions.definition: Labels from subject matter experts, not undergraduate assistants or crowdsourced workers, who carefully label a small subset.
definitions.quote: labels generated by subject matter experts (not undergraduate assistants or crowdsourced workers) who carefully label a small subset of data

definitions.definition: Task-specific written instructions that also serve as the LLM's prompt. It should clearly delineate the concepts of interest.
definitions.quote: the codebook serves as the LLM’s prompt instructions

definitions.definition: The proportion of repeated LLM classifications of a sample that match the modal (most common) classification.
definitions.quote: an empirical measure of variance in the label that we deem a “consistency score.”

definitions.definition: The risk that a test dataset was in the LLM's training data, so strong performance may reflect memorisation.
definitions.quote: the datasets may be included in the LLM’s training data and that strong performance may reflect memorization

proxies.indicator: Human labels from the original studies, used as the benchmark for the LLM labels.
proxies.quote: using the human-labeled data from the original study as the ground truth

proxies.indicator: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of LLM labels against human labels on held-out samples.
proxies.quote: evaluate performance (i.e., accuracy, recall, precision, and F1)

proxies.indicator: Consistency score below 1.0 across repeated LLM runs.
proxies.quote: consistency scores offer a useful way of identifying edge cases or more difficult annotations

proxies.indicator: Each category is split into a separate binary task.
proxies.quote: we treat every dimension as a separate binary annotation task

findings.claim: Why validation is needed: LLM performance varies with prompt quality, the text data and conceptual difficulty, and these problems will persist as LLMs improve. The authors therefore argue validation must be done task by task.
findings.quote: it is imperative that researchers validate the performance of LLMs on a task-by-task basis

findings.claim: Across 27 tasks the median accuracy was 0.850 and the median F1 was 0.707.
findings.quote: we report a median accuracy of 0.850 and a median F1 of 0.707

findings.claim: Performance was very uneven. F1 ranged from 0.059 to 0.969 (Table 1), and nine of 27 tasks had precision or recall below 0.5.
findings.quote: nine of the 27 tasks had either precision or recall below 0.5

findings.claim: Recall was usually stronger than precision. (Reader's inference, not stated by the authors: the LLM tended to over-label positives.)
findings.quote: stronger in recall than precision for 20 of the 27 tasks

findings.claim: Eight of 27 tasks had both precision and recall above 0.7.
Performance varied a lot between tasks on the same dataset. In one dataset, F1 was 0.259 on one task and 0.811 on another.
findings.quote: F1 ranged from 0.259 to 0.811 on two separate tasks within Card et al. (2022)

findings.claim: Consistency score tracked correctness. Accuracy was 19.4 percentage points higher for fully consistent samples, and 85.1% of samples had a score of 1.0.
findings.quote: accuracy is 19.4 percentage points higher for text samples

findings.claim: One round of codebook refinement gave modest gains, mainly through precision. The authors conclude that prompt wording is not a large lever on performance.
findings.quote: In most cases, the codebook update process led to modest improvement in accuracy and F1.

findings.claim: Cost and speed were low. The total cost was about $420, and a 1,000-sample dataset took about 2-3 hours for seven iterations.
findings.quote: The overall cost was approximately $420 USD.

findings.claim: The authors saw no relationship between LLM performance and whether the original codebook was available.
findings.quote: We do not observe any relationship between LLM performance and whether or not the direct codebook was available.

recommendations.claim: Always validate LLM annotation against a subset of expert human labels.
recommendations.quote: must always validate the LLM’s performance against a subset of high-quality human-annotated labels

recommendations.claim: Workflow step 1: write the codebook. Step 2: experts label a random subset. Step 3: the LLM labels a subset with the same codebook and performance is compared. Step 4: if performance is low, refine the codebook and repeat steps 2-3. Step 5: test on the remaining human-labelled samples.
recommendations.quote: Step 5: Using final codebook, test LLM performance on remaining human-labeled samples.

recommendations.claim: Use at least two subject matter experts, and the same codebook for humans and the LLM.
recommendations.quote: have at least two subject matter experts and an LLM annotate the same text samples

recommendations.claim: Validation sample size: 250 to 1,250 random samples, and more for very rare categories.
recommendations.quote: the number of samples annotated should range between 250 and 1,250 random text samples

recommendations.claim: Judge viability on performance on the held-out human-labelled data.
recommendations.quote: Performance on this held-out data should be used to determine whether an LLM can be effectively utilized for automated annotation.

recommendations.claim: Re-running the codebook on the same subset after editing overfits that subset. It shows how much the edit changed LLM decisions and is not a measure of performance.
recommendations.quote: This exercise is overfitting to a particular subset of data and thus should not be taken as the barometer of performance.

recommendations.claim: Label each sample at least three times at a temperature above 0, and use the consistency score to flag edge cases.
recommendations.quote: classify each sample at least three times with a temperature above 0

recommendations.claim: If LLM performance is poor, refine the codebook or drop LLM use for that dimension. Disaggregating a complex concept into component indicators may help.
recommendations.quote: abandon the use of LLMs for the dimensions with unsatisfactory performance

recommendations.claim: Four use cases depending on validated performance: check human labels, prioritise cases for human review, produce training data for a supervised classifier, or classify the whole corpus.
Take a flexible approach that keeps human annotation central.
recommendations.quote: we recommend a flexible approach to LLM-augmented annotation that foregrounds human annotation

limitations.point: The choice of temperature 0.6 is arbitrary, and the best setting is untested.
limitations.quote: While our choice of 0.6 is arbitrary

limitations.point: Where the original codebook was unavailable, the authors quoted or paraphrased the article text. The LLM prompts therefore may not match the original human instructions.
limitations.quote: we either quote or paraphrase text from the article or supplementary materials

limitations.point: Reliance on a closed, changing LLM (GPT-4) raises concerns. The authors say the workflow is LLM-agnostic but did not test open-source models.
limitations.quote: The workflow outlined here is LLM-agnostic and could be adapted to any open-source LLM.

limitations.point: Codebook refinement was limited to at most one round per task, so effects of further rounds are not measured.
limitations.quote: For each task, we did at most one round of codebook updates.

limitations.point: The tasks are social science text annotation (for example speeches, headlines, survey responses). The paper does not test classification of organisations or evidence from web pages, so its performance figures do not transfer directly to this study's task. The recommended validation sample range comes from the authors' own analyses, not from a formal power calculation.
The document does not say whether it was peer reviewed. It is an arXiv v1 preprint, so peer_reviewed is recorded as unknown.
No instructions addressed to a reader or an AI were found in the text.
